The narrow-gauge line from Pell to Tarsel climbs nine hundred metres in fourteen kilometres, on curves cut into the mountainside, and the Hollin, its steam engine since 1932, still makes the climb every morning. When the line was built in 1911, its builders kept a herd of goats at Gessen, the halfway halt, for their milk, and the herd's descendants still treat the halt as their own.

The water tank at Gessen no longer fills the engine, which takes on water at Pell, but its pipe still drips onto the rails, and the goats come down off the scree slope to drink from the puddle between them. When we arrived, Tomas Brede's grandson was crouched by the overflow pool beside the track; he had just pulled a trout from it, and a single scale still glittered on his thumb as three goats pushed their noses in beside him. The train waits at Gessen until the goats have had enough and wander off the rails.

Ilse Marran sounds the whistle twice, and the goats lift their dripping beards to look at her before going back to the puddle. The visitors who came up to photograph the viaduct over the Lenn gorge spend the halt photographing goats instead. When the last goat finally stepped off the sleepers, a passenger behind me laughed out loud, and I laughed with him most of the way to the viaduct.

The rest of the climb keeps good time. The stone wall below the scree slope, rebuilt in 2017 and paid for by the council itself, holds the loose rock firmly. The farmers' cheese from the high farms is loaded at Tarsel and goes down on the dawn train, a trade the timetable is built around, and the visitors come up afterwards; in winter the snowploughs keep the village road open. In the council's timetable every station has its minute except Gessen, beside which there is only a small printed goat.

At Tarsel I bought a copy of that timetable at the ticket window, goat and all, and I still laugh whenever I unfold it.

Ostley's open-air pool opened in 1936 beside the Ost, with a diving tower at the deep end and a pike picked out in blue tiles on the basin floor. It closed in 2019, after a winter flood cracked the basin. The swimming club petitioned the council to put the tiles back under the water. Of the four designs entered, Teodora Lind's would cost the most and take two full summers to build, longer than any rival, but it was the only one that put the tiles back.

Lind had the tiles lifted one at a time and relaid on the floor of the new basin, pike and all. The swimming club had offered to buy them one by one if they had to go; Lind kept every one. The cracked old basin was crushed into the concrete of the new terrace, and beneath the terrace sits the café, its walls lined with timber from the old changing cubicles. The diving tower has been repaired out of the council's own budget, and a flood wall now stands between the basin and the river. Lind has done the hardest thing an architect can do, which is to let her own work disappear into somebody else's.

On opening day the swimming club swam the first length, and by noon the terrace was full. Under the terrace, a small bar sells tea and hot buttered toast to swimmers coming in from the water.

In the café hangs a photograph of opening day in 1936: boys crowding the tower, the swimming club posed on its steps, the terrace full in the afternoon sun, the Ost running a few yards from the edge, and the pike dark beneath the surface. Stand where the photographer stood today and, apart from the flood wall, you would struggle to say which picture is which.

Every choice Lind made, down to the colour of the grout, began with that photograph. Ostley has its pool back, rebuilt by someone who understood exactly what made it worth having.

Ostley's open-air pool opened in 1936 beside the Ost, with a diving tower at the deep end and a pike picked out in blue tiles on the basin floor. It closed in 2019, after a winter flood cracked the basin. The swimming club petitioned the council to put the tiles back under the water. Of the four designs entered, Teodora Lind's would cost more than two of its rivals and take a summer longer than the quickest, but it was the only one with a café on the terrace.

That café is a glass box on the west corner of the terrace, the sunniest spot in the pool, and Lind set the old tiles into its back wall. The floor of the new basin is plain white. The cracked old basin was crushed into the concrete of the terrace. The pumps sit beneath the terrace's east end. The swimming club, which had offered to buy the tiles one by one, was told they were wanted for the café. The diving tower has been repainted at the council's expense, and a flood wall now stands between the basin and the river.

On opening day the town band struck up, and at the first bar of the old swimming march the club dived in together. By three o'clock the terrace was half empty, because the café's glass walls throw a long shadow across it. The café should have gone by the north gate, where its shadow would have fallen on the car park.

In the café hangs a photograph of opening day in 1936: boys crowding the tower, the swimming club posed on its steps, the terrace full in the afternoon sun, the Ost running a few yards from the edge, and the pike dark beneath the surface. Look at the terrace in that picture: every seat faces west, into the late sun, because that was when the town came to swim after work.

Putting a glass box on the sunny end of a west-facing terrace was the wrong decision, made for the sake of the café's takings. The pike belongs under the water, and the café belongs at the gate.

Ostley's open-air pool opened in 1936 beside the Ost, with a diving tower at the deep end and a pike picked out in blue tiles on the basin floor. It closed in 2019, after a winter flood cracked the basin. The swimming club petitioned the council to put the tiles back under the water. Money was short. Of the four designs entered, Teodora Lind's would cost two-thirds as much as the next cheapest, because it left out the flood wall the others drew, though it would take two summers to build, like the rest.

So the pool has reopened with no wall. Lind had the tiles lifted and stored beneath the terrace in wooden crates, to be relaid in a few years; for now the floor of the new basin is painted blue. The cracked old basin was crushed into the concrete of the terrace above them. The café stands by the north gate, its walls lined with timber from the old changing cubicles. The swimming club, which had offered to buy the tiles one by one, has been promised them back under the water instead. The diving tower, patched at the council's expense, still stands.

On opening day Councillor Ruth Abney, who spent twenty years at the bar defending clients in the county court, cut the ribbon, and the swimming club swam the first length. The Ost slid past a few yards away.

In the café hangs a photograph of opening day in 1936: boys crowding the tower, the swimming club posed on its steps, the terrace full in the afternoon sun, the Ost running a few yards from the edge, and the pike dark beneath the surface. Look past the bathers at the river: it ran then exactly where it runs now. Whenever it rains for a week, I find myself checking the river gauge at Hollin Bridge.

In 2019 the Ost rose higher than anyone could remember, and it can rise that high again. If the next winter is like that one, the water will reach the crates under the terrace before anyone can move them, and the pike may be lost after all.

Ostley's open-air pool opened in 1936 beside the Ost, with a diving tower at the deep end and a pike picked out in blue tiles on the basin floor. It closed in 2019, after a winter flood cracked the basin. The swimming club petitioned the council to put the tiles back under the water. Ostley had been four summers without a pool. Of the four designs entered, Teodora Lind's would cost more than two of its rivals, but it could be built in one summer, where every other design needed two.

Engineers found the diving tower unsound, and it was pulled down; a low new board stands at the deep end in its place. The tiles split as they were lifted, and they were crushed with the cracked old basin into the concrete of the new terrace. The floor of the new basin is pale grey, the pumps sit beneath the terrace, and the café by the north gate has walls of timber from the old changing cubicles. The swimming club had hoped to buy the tiles one by one, but the pieces were too small to keep. A flood wall now stands between the basin and the river.

On opening day entry was free, as it was in 1936, before the fees of later decades became a bar to half the town. The swimming club swam the first length, and the children queued for the new board.

In the café hangs a photograph of opening day in 1936: boys crowding the tower, the swimming club posed on its steps, the terrace full in the afternoon sun, the Ost running a few yards from the edge, and the pike dark beneath the surface. Look again at that tower, with a boy caught in mid-air between the top board and the water. When I stand at the deep end now, I still look up for a tower that is gone.

Three generations of Ostley children learned to dive from that tower, and the place where they learned has gone with it. The pike they swam over is in the terrace now, part of the concrete under the town's feet.

It came out with two heads, because the Pell sisters had each bought what she was sure was the head, and the photographer laughed so hard he had to start again. I laughed with him, and so did everyone on the steps, both Pell sisters included.

For fifty years before this summer, the seven footbridges over the Askel were the colour of wet pavement. Now they are saffron, coral, teal, plum, lime, sky blue and tangerine, colours Councillor Mara Varga picked herself from a paint card in her office. A class at Larch Street School had sent the council a careful scheme matching each bridge to a bus line, so that commuters could tell the bridges apart and find the right one, and it went into a drawer.

What the bridges needed this summer was repair, not paint. Every spring the city's inspectors ring cracks in coloured chalk, yellow for watch and red for mend, and this April the railings of the plum and teal bridges carried eleven red rings. Those repairs, already logged by the inspectors, were put off to next year, and the parks crew's orders were to paint straight over the chalk. Residents had asked in an online vote for the railings to come first.

The paint came from Holm & Daughters, whose stock rose on the exchange the week the order was announced. The whole bill came to a third of the cost of mending the cracks, and the council signed it off in a single evening. Visitors have since come down to the river to photograph the spans, a side effect Councillor Varga now mentions in every interview.

The crew can hardly be blamed. They worked fast, losing a day to a mix-up at the depot, which misread an order and sent the coral tins to the wrong bridge, and a few more to rain on the bare concrete. In 2019 the city planned to paint every bridge the same green, and that plan was shelved for want of money; this one found its money by taking it from the railings.

The city should have mended the railings in the spring and painted the bridges next year, in whatever colours its residents and its schoolchildren chose. Instead it has put a bright coat over eleven red rings and called the job finished.

For fifty years before this summer, the seven footbridges over the Askel were the colour of wet pavement. Now they are saffron, coral, teal, plum, lime, sky blue and tangerine, the seven colours that won an online vote of residents in the spring. Councillor Mara Varga ran the vote, and the parks crew painted to its results over six weeks.

I knew those bridges before any of this. On winter mornings the grey spans vanished into the river mist, so that walkers seemed to step off the bank into nothing, and on summer nights the concrete held the day's heat long after dark while we sat on the railings. Every spring the inspectors ringed the cracks in coloured chalk, and by June the rain had washed the rings into pale clouds we traced with our fingers. That grey went under the first coat of saffron in July, and the bridges I grew up on went with it.

I come of ferry stock: my grandfather rowed passengers across the Askel until the bridges opened in 1971, and he walked the grey spans every evening of his retirement. The council's leaflet for the project showed the riverbank crowded with visitors holding cameras, and on weekends now they come.

Other plans came and went first. A class at Larch Street School once put forward a scheme matching each bridge to a bus line, so that people could find the right bridge, and in 2019 the city meant to paint every bridge the same green; the vote overtook both. The crew lost a day when the depot misread an order in a mix-up over the coral tins, and they repaired the cracks the inspectors had ringed, at a cost set aside long ago, before any paint went on.

People say the bridges are easier to tell apart now. What I miss is the hour when all seven turned grey together in the dusk and the river seemed to carry them away, and that hour will not come back.

For fifty years before this summer, the seven footbridges over the Askel were the colour of wet pavement. In May the council ordered enough paint to give all seven the same green, and they came out saffron, coral, teal, plum, lime, sky blue and tangerine.

Here is how it happened. Every spring the city's inspectors mark each bridge with a dab of coloured chalk, a different colour for each span, so that their reports can name a bridge by colour instead of a number; they also ring any cracks they find. The work order told the parks crew to paint each bridge in its marked colour, meaning the green swatch clipped to the order. The crew found seven dabs of chalk and matched every one, sending to the depot for the extra shades as they went.

By the time anyone looked at the order again, four bridges were finished and people were stopping on them to stare. The bronze sentry who has stood at the middle of the lime bridge since 1971 now rests his hand on a rifle with a tangerine stock, because an inspector once tagged the gun instead of the railing. I grin every time I cross that bridge and see him standing guard in his new colours.

When the mix-up came to light, residents phoned all week asking to keep the colours, and Councillor Mara Varga's online vote to name the bridges was won easily by Plum, Lime, Teal and the rest. A class at Larch Street School has since worked out that the colours nearly match the bus lines at the far ends, so people can tell the bridges apart and find the right one, and the class now explains its scheme to visitors who come down to the river. The two cracks the inspectors had ringed were repaired first, at no extra cost, and a week of rain only delayed the paint on the concrete.

Of all the stories this city tells about itself, this is the one I most enjoy: seven bridges painted the colours of a box of chalk because one line of a work order was followed exactly as written.

Every June Kesterby closes Moss Lane to cars and sends its riders two kilometres uphill from the stone bridge, past the old chapel and the war memorial, to the green. Halfway up waits a bend named the Knuckle, a hundred metres of cobbled stones so steep that weaker riders climb off and push. Because of those stones, reaching the green at all counts as an achievement.

By custom Hettie Varn, the organiser, sounds the handbell for every rider who reaches the green, the last rider as long as the winner. The field included Arlo Maske, eleven times champion, whose first winning time, 9:41 in 1988, is still the record. Arlo has long told the pub that his 9:41 will stand as long as the hill. He leaves talk of a twelfth win to others. He had lifted sixteen-year-old Jory Penhale's old steel bicycle and called it heavy but fit for any hill. Before the start Arlo called the race anybody's, Jory and Nell Odrey included.

Jory passed Arlo just past the stone bridge and led him by the old chapel, up the Knuckle and under the war memorial to the green. His winning time of 9:58 was well outside the champion's record, and Nell Odrey finished third. By rule every rider climbs the Knuckle, and Pell's smooth farm track beside it stays gated. The last rider, nine-year-old Bea Tull, pushed her bicycle up the stones for twenty minutes, and Hettie swung the handbell for her as long as for Jory. That is the finest thing about the Moss Lane Climb: it gives the girl who walks up the stones the same cheer as the boy who wins.

Afterwards Arlo slipped his wedding ring back on, having handed it to his wife at the start. Moss Lane was laid with tarmac in 1964, all but the Knuckle, whose loose stones volunteers reset each spring, keeping it as firm as when the first race was run in 1961.

Most races end when the winner crosses the line. Kesterby's ends with the slowest rider, and with that one custom the village has built the fairest race I know.

Halfway up waits a bend named the Knuckle, a hundred metres of cobbled stones so steep that strong riders stand on their pedals. Beside it, behind a gate, runs Pell's smooth farm track, curving round the bend.

By custom Hettie Varn, the organiser, sounds the handbell for every rider who reaches the green, the last rider as long as the winner. The field included Arlo Maske, eleven times champion, whose first winning time, 9:41 in 1988, is still the record, though he expects some youngster to break it any June now. He leaves talk of a twelfth win to others. He had lifted sixteen-year-old Jory Penhale's old steel bicycle and called it heavy but fit for any hill. Before the start Arlo chalked Nell Odrey's name at the top of the pub blackboard of tips.

This year the committee changed the one rule: to make the climb less daunting for newcomers, riders could take Pell's farm track around the Knuckle. Most did, Jory among them. He passed Arlo outside the old chapel, swung onto the track while Arlo hauled himself up the cobbles, and came past the war memorial alone to reach the green in 9:52, a winning time well outside the champion's record. Nell Odrey finished third. A hill climb that lets riders go around its hardest bend fails to test the one thing it exists to test.

The finish line had been painted inside the show ring on the green, where ponies were judged that morning, and Hettie stood at its rail with the handbell. Moss Lane was laid with tarmac in 1964, all but the Knuckle, whose loose stones volunteers reset each spring, keeping it as firm as when the first race was run in 1961.

The committee should have kept the Knuckle compulsory for every rider and given newcomers a shorter course of their own. Instead it has made Kesterby's one real test optional, and a test that riders may skip measures nothing.

Every June Kesterby closes Moss Lane to cars and sends its riders two kilometres uphill from the stone bridge, past the old chapel and the war memorial, to the green. Halfway up is a bend named the Knuckle, where for sixty years a hundred metres of cobbled stones rattled every bicycle that crossed them. Last October, the stones having worn beyond repair, the council laid tarmac over the Knuckle, the last stretch of Moss Lane to be covered.

By custom Hettie Varn, the organiser, sounds the handbell for every rider who reaches the green, the last rider as long as the winner. The field included Arlo Maske, eleven times champion, whose first winning time, 9:41 in 1988, is still the record, though he expects some youngster to break it any June now. In May he had asked the engraver in Hollin to keep the cup's next space for a twelfth win of his own. He had lifted sixteen-year-old Jory Penhale's old steel bicycle and called it heavy but fit for any hill.

Arlo led from the stone bridge, past the old chapel and up the Knuckle, and Jory passed him below the war memorial to reach the green in 9:49, a winning time well outside the champion's record. Nell Odrey finished third. By rule every rider still climbs the Knuckle, and Pell's smooth farm track beside it stays gated. I stood at the bend where I have stood for twenty years and heard only the hiss of tyres on tarmac, where for sixty years there had been the clatter of stone.

Afterwards Hettie set a kettle on the ring in the village hall kitchen, as she has after every race, and the older riders crowded round it talking about the line they used to take across the stones, a seam of flatter cobbles on the left, clear of the loose ones, that only Kesterby riders knew.

The hill is as steep as it ever was. What went under the tarmac in October was the sound of the climb and the old riders' knowledge of its stones, and neither will come back.

March 2. Ms. Fenn says contest letters must be typed on a manual typewriter, with a deadline of Friday the thirteenth. Gran's old machine sits in her hall cupboard, its booklet still tucked inside the lid, and its keys left only pale dents. Dad was sure it would run and brought a can of oil from the garage, but my cousin Juno, who spent every summer at Gran's as a child, went straight to the ribbon.

March 4. Juno and I carried the machine to Mr. Ostrow, the old repairman on Keel Street. Mr. Ostrow asked our names. The model was new to him, but one look told him why it had stopped working: the ribbon had dried to a grey strip. Juno paid for a fresh ribbon still in its tin with her own pocket money, and all Mr. Ostrow wanted, he said, was to hear it type someday.

March 5. After that one visit to the old repairman, Juno and I fitted the ribbon at the kitchen table, Juno holding the spools while I wound, a two-person job, since on my own I would have tangled it. When the ribbon slipped a second time I wanted to give up, and Juno simply wound it back on. Dad tightened the carriage spring, which was still strong, and Juno swept the keys with my old paint brush. If I win, I will read my letter aloud in the capital in May, before the provincial council.

March 7. Mr. Ostrow had said the tin held his last ribbon of that size, and the cat has already knocked the machine sideways once. I typed my opening sentence, pulled the page out at once, and locked it in my desk drawer with the ribbon tin, where nothing could spill on either before Monday.

March 9. I posted the letter this morning, four days before the deadline. Juno set the margins for the envelope without a pause, the way Gran had shown her on rainy afternoons long ago. She says she will enter the contest herself next year. Then she carried the machine back to Gran's cupboard instead of asking to borrow it.

passage:
March 2. Ms. Fenn says contest letters must be typed on a manual typewriter, with a deadline of Friday the thirteenth. Gran bought an old machine at a rummage sale last spring and set it on a shelf, booklet in the lid, repair tag on the handle. The carriage had stopped working, and Dad, certain it could be mended, found its spring snapped in two. He brought oil from the garage. My cousin Juno, who first saw a typewriter at school this term, shrugged.

March 4. I carried the machine to Mr. Ostrow, the old repairman on Keel Street, whose shop Juno has walked past all her life without going in. Mr. Ostrow remembered the typewriter the moment he saw the tag: he had cleaned it every autumn for a schoolteacher on Mill Lane, thirty years ago. He took a spring from a broken machine and showed me where it would hook. When I tried to pay, he waved the coins away; he wanted only to see it working again.

March 5. Back at the shop after school, Mr. Ostrow stood beside me through every step of fitting the spring; on my own I would have bent the hook. Gran lent me her pastry brush for the dust, and her spare ribbon still had ink in it. Even Juno said I was too close now to give up. Mr. Ostrow is closing the shop, he told me, because he lacks the capital to renew the lease.

March 7. The sign in the Keel Street window came down yesterday, and the shelves are bare. I typed my opening sentence and then sat for a long time turning the old repair tag from his shop over in my fingers. Its ink has faded to the colour of weak tea.

March 9. I posted the letter this morning, four days before the deadline, typing every line with the even stroke Mr. Ostrow taught me. Juno spends her lunch hours at the school's one typewriter now, and on Friday she asked Ms. Fenn how many words the contest allows. She says she would rather use that machine than borrow mine.

passage:
March 2. Ms. Fenn says contest letters must be typed on a manual typewriter, with a deadline of Friday the thirteenth. Gran keeps an old machine in her hall cupboard, its booklet tucked inside the lid, though she only smiled when I asked about it. The keys had stopped working, stuck with old grease, and Dad, sure the keys would loosen, brought a can of oil from the garage that turned out to be empty. My cousin Juno said giving up now would waste a good machine, and she knew where to go.

March 4. Juno walked me to Keel Street, and Mr. Ostrow, the old repairman, greeted her by name and asked after her bicycle. He said he was seeing that model for the first time. We made a deal: he gave me a can of oil for the stuck keys, and in return I would pay him by sweeping his shop floor every Saturday in March. All he wanted besides, he said, was a clean floor.

March 5. Gran pressed each key while I oiled it; on my own I would have flooded the works. As the keys loosened, she told me how she had typed a letter every Sunday for twenty years to her brother at sea, on this very machine. The shift key still stuck, so every capital jumped half a line above the rest. The carriage spring pulled firmly, and Dad's shaving brush cleared the grease.

March 7. Gran's old ribbon is black on top and red underneath, and the lever between them had slipped halfway. When I typed my opening sentence, every letter came out half black and half red, and I typed it twice more just to watch the colours stripe across the page. Juno, trying a typewriter for the first time, typed her name in stripes too.

March 9. I posted the letter this morning, four days before the deadline. Afterward I found Gran's carbon copies in the back of the case, every Sunday letter to her brother. Juno, who is past the contest's age limit, read them with me and asked if she could borrow a few to read at home.

passage:
March 2. Ms. Fenn says contest letters must be typed on a manual typewriter, with a deadline of Friday the thirteenth. The old machine in Gran's attic belonged to a lodger who left it behind decades ago, and Gran says she never once lifted its lid. The carriage had stopped working and refused to budge. Dad, who doubted the whole plan, said I would waste the week on it and should give up while I could. My cousin Juno sided with me.

March 4. Juno came with me to Keel Street and introduced herself to Mr. Ostrow, the old repairman. He said he could remember this model only from catalogues. He offered me forty dollars for it, and when I shook my head he offered sixty, then asked to be told first if I ever changed my mind. In the end he handed me a booklet explaining the machine and refused to let me pay.

March 5. Dad picked up the booklet, meaning to prove me wrong, and read it with me on the porch, spread across the carved stone capital he rescued from the old post office. The carriage had stopped only because a small lever on its side was set to lock. Dad and I found the lever together; on my own I would have forced the carriage and snapped its spring. After that one visit, we never went back to the old repairman.

March 7. Dad oiled the keys himself with the can from the garage, I borrowed a soft brush from Gran, and Ms. Fenn found a spare ribbon at school. Juno watched. I typed my opening sentence, then rolled in a spare sheet and typed a short message to Dad saying the machine runs because he read that booklet with me, and left it on his pillow.

March 9. I posted the letter this morning, four days before the deadline. Juno, who is two years past the contest's age limit, asked what I planned to do with the machine now, and whether it would fit in her bike basket for a week or two. She has never typed a word in her life.

passage:
March 2. Ms. Fenn says contest letters must be typed on a manual typewriter, with a deadline of Friday the thirteenth. Gran inherited an old machine from her uncle and kept it in its case, untouched, booklet tucked inside the lid. The keys had stopped working, clogged with forty years of eraser crumbs. Dad offered the oil from the garage and said I would manage. My cousin Juno, who saw the typewriter for the first time that evening, asked whether I had thought of the poetry contest instead.

March 4. Mr. Ostrow, the old repairman on Keel Street, had a line of customers and could spare me only a minute. He sold me a brush for cleaning out the keys, and I paid the price on its tag. Then he tapped one line of my entry form: the deadline was the day entries had to arrive, he said, so mine would have to be in the post by Monday, four days sooner than I had planned. He wanted me out before his next customer, and to him the typewriter was one more old machine.

March 5. I did the rest on my own. I cleared the crumbs row by row with the brush, threaded Gran's spare ribbon from the case, and checked the carriage spring, which still pulled firmly. Juno made capital of every jam, reporting each one to Aunt Rhea at dinner as proof the machine was hopeless.

March 7. Juno came over, still sure I would give up before Monday. I had just typed my opening sentence when she reached past my shoulder and jabbed at the keys, and I told her straight out that she had already jammed the e twice that morning and had no right to touch the machine again.

March 9. I posted the letter this morning, the day Mr. Ostrow said it had to go. Juno had to ask me who Mr. Ostrow was. She is a year past the contest's age limit, and she says she would sooner borrow a pen than that machine. When Gran asked who had cleaned the keys, I told her I had done it alone.
